title: Information capacity of quantum statistics: Fock-state tests of a discrete binary-sequence model on cloud photonic quantum processors
authors: Chiran Wijesundara, Octavia T. Volpe, Dejan Stojkovic, Herbert Fotso, Tim Thomay
abstract: Our central premise is that quantum mechanics may be the statistical limit of a more fundamental discrete theory: any such theory equips a physical system with a finite information capacity, and its departure from quantum statistics is controlled by how much of that capacity the system uses. We show that commercial cloud photonic quantum processors have reached the precision required to bound this capacity from below, using the binary-sequence model of Powers et al. as the concrete test theory: outcome probabilities arise from counting discrete sequences of length $n$, quantum mechanics is recovered as $n \to \infty$, and $n$ measures the information capacity of the register behind a prepared state. Photon Fock states $|1\rangle$, $|1,1\rangle$, heralded $|2\rangle$, and cascaded beam-splitter pairs are measured on programmable interferometers with dominant systematics determined in situ. The model's composition-consistent parametrization, singled out by requiring that rotations compose, recovers quantum mechanics with deviations $1.24/n$; a random-effects likelihood analysis calibrated by parametric bootstrap excludes all $n \le 100$: the information capacity of the register carrying the two-photon state, if finite, exceeds $10^2$. Cascaded beam splitters test the composition law directly: the data are split-invariant, excluding naive count composition at $8σ$ and confirming the interference-sign rule. Model-independently, curve-averaged deviations from the quantum partition law larger than $2.3\times10^{-2}$ are excluded at 95% CL, and the originally published linear parametrization is excluded outright. Because the compilation offset is frozen per circuit it is calibratable, opening the $10^{-3}$ floor ($n \sim 10^3$) to current hardware: cloud photonic processors are quantitative instruments for quantum foundations, and information capacity an experimentally boundable quantity.
summary: This paper uses cloud photonic quantum processors to test the hypothesis that quantum mechanics emerges as a statistical limit from a discrete underlying theory. By analyzing photon Fock state measurements, the authors constrain the information capacity of the physical register, ruling out simpler discrete models and demonstrating that this capacity can be experimentally quantified.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum mechanics is the statistical limit of a more fundamental discrete theory by quantifying the information capacity of the underlying physical system.
main_result: Experimental tests using cloud photonic quantum processors exclude discrete models with information capacities less than $10^2$, establishing that information capacity is an experimentally boundable quantity.
method: The authors employed random-effects likelihood analysis and differential tests on photon Fock states measured on programmable interferometers to compare measured outcome probabilities against predictions from the discrete binary-sequence model versus quantum mechanics.
model_or_system: The physical system is commercial cloud photonic quantum processors utilizing photon Fock states. The theoretical model tested is the binary-sequence model of Powers et al., which predicts quantum statistics in the limit of infinite sequence length ($n 	o \infty$).
key_observables: Outcome probabilities, deviation from the quantum partition law, and the sequence length $n$ (interpreted as information capacity).
important_parameters: The information capacity bound ($>10^2$), the scaling of deviations ($1.24/n$), and the statistical floor ($10^{-3}$).
main_assumptions: Systematics (like calibration offsets and source indistinguishability) are determined *in situ* and treated as nuisance parameters; the composition-consistent parametrization is assumed to be the correct physical description.
figures_summary: Figures compare sequence-model vs. QM partition probabilities for various inputs and show the dependence of model deviation on sequence length $n$ and different analysis conditions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the theoretical premise (QM as a statistical limit), detailing the experimental setup and model (binary-sequence model), presenting rigorous statistical tests (random-effects likelihood, differential tests), and concluding with the quantitative bounds on information capacity.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges quantum foundations with experimental quantum optics, providing a concrete, measurable test for the fundamental nature of quantum statistics using current photonic hardware.
